Others said: this verse does not have the meaning of that one; rather, this is a promise to make him recite the Law and the surahs, and He commanded him not to forget, in the sense of steadfastness and emphasis, and Allah the Exalted knew that avoiding forgetting is not within his power, so it is a prohibition against neglecting constant review. His saying: "And We will ease you toward ease" means: We will take you toward the praiseworthy matters in your worldly life and your Hereafter, of victory, triumph, the elevation of your message and station on the Day of Resurrection, and exaltation in Paradise.

Tafsir of Surat al-A'la

It is Meccan according to the majority. Al-Naqqash related from al-Dahhak that it is Medinan, but that is weak. What prompted this view was the statement of those who said that it mentions the Eid prayer in it.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

"Aflaḥa" (succeeded) in this verse means: he attained his desire. "Tazakkā" (purified himself) means: he purified his soul and made it grow with good. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah' purifies himself from shirk." Al-Hasan said: whoever's deeds are pure (zākiyan). Abu al-Ahwas said: whoever gives generously from his wealth and purifies it.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord﴾ means: he declared His oneness and prayed to Him the prayers that were prescribed for him, and he also performed voluntary prayer and good deeds as much as he was able. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn 'Umar, and Ibn al-Musayyab said: this verse refers to the morning of the day of Fitr, so "tazakkā" means he paid the zakat al-fitr, ﴿and remembers the name of his Lord﴾ means he remembered Allah the Exalted on the way to the musalla until the imam came out, and "al-salah" is (p-594) the Eid prayer. Abu 'Amr alone read "yu'thirūna" with the ya' (they prefer), and said: it refers to the two wretched ones (al-ashaqqayn). This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', and al-Jahdari. The cause of preferring is love of what is immediate and ignorance of the enduring nature of the Hereafter. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "What is in the world, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing but the puff of a hare."

His saying, the Exalted: "Inna hādhā" (indeed, this). Al-Dahhak said: it refers to the Qur'an. It is related that the Qur'an was copied from the former scriptures. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: it refers to the meanings of this surah. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to these two reports: the success of the one who purifies himself, and people's preference for the world despite the superiority of the Hereafter over it. This is the most preferred view because of the nearness of what is pointed to by "hādhā" (this).

Meaning: it is among what the earlier ones brought and which continued in the others.

The majority read "al-ṣuḥufu" with a ḍammah on the ḥā', and Harun related from Abu 'Amr the sukun on the ḥā', which is the reading of al-A'mash. Abu Raja' read "Ibrahm" without a yā' or alif, Ibn al-Zubayr read "Ibrāhām," and likewise Abu Musa al-Ash'ari in the whole Qur'an. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr read "Ibrahim" with a kasrah on the hā' and without a yā' throughout the Qur'an.

It is related that the scrolls of Abraham, peace be upon him, were revealed on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth of Ramadan, the Psalms on the twelfth of it, the Gospel on the eighteenth of it, and the Qur'an on the fourteenth of it.

The commentary of Surah [al-A'la] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
